pharm: Equimolar mixture of dextrose (glucose) and fructose given intravenously as a source of carbohydrate calories and water for hydration.
tags: Not a separately FDA-approved branded drug
quick: Individualized; typically 5-10% invert sugar solution IV titrated to caloric/fluid needs (e.g., commonly up to 5-10 g/kg/day)
Intravenous infusion; provides calories when oral intake is inadequate
Use if clearly needed for fluid/caloric support; monitor glucose
Monitor fluid balance and electrolytes; caution in oliguria
Blood glucose, fluid balance, electrolytes, infusion site
summary: Invert sugar is an equimolar mixture of dextrose (glucose) and fructose, produced by hydrolysis (inversion) of sucrose. Given as an intravenous solution (commonly 5% or 10%), it serves as a source of carbohydrate calories and water for parenteral hydration and partial caloric support when oral or enteral intake is inadequate. The fructose component can be metabolized partly independent of insulin, which historically was thought advantageous, but invert sugar is now uncommon and is CONTRAINDICATED in hereditary fructose intolerance, where fructose can cause severe hypoglycemia and acute liver failure. Doses are individualized to the patient's fluid, electrolyte, and caloric needs, with monitoring of blood glucose, fluid balance, and electrolytes. NOTE: invert sugar is largely a compendial (USP) parenteral solution rather than a distinct branded FDA-approved drug, and its clinical use is now limited.
indications: Source of water and carbohydrate calories for parenteral hydration
Caloric supplementation when oral or enteral intake is inadequate
Vehicle/diluent for compatible intravenous medications (per labeling)

dosage.d: Individualized; 5% or 10% invert sugar solution infused to meet fluid and caloric needs (carbohydrate load commonly limited to avoid exceeding metabolic utilization, e.g., not exceeding ~0.5 g/kg/hour)
Individualized by weight, fluid, and caloric requirements with close glucose monitoring

admin: Administer by intravenous infusion only; inspect for clarity and absence of particulate matter before use
Control the infusion rate to avoid hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis, and fluid overload
Use aseptic technique; monitor the infusion site for infiltration, phlebitis, or extravasation
Do not use if hereditary fructose intolerance is known or suspected
Discard any unused portion; do not store partially used containers for later use
moa: Invert sugar provides the monosaccharides glucose and fructose in equimolar amounts. Glucose is utilized by virtually all tissues as a primary energy substrate. Fructose is metabolized predominantly in the liver (and to a lesser extent kidney and intestine) and enters glycolysis/gluconeogenesis largely independent of insulin in its initial steps. The infused carbohydrate supplies calories (about 4 kcal/g) and, with the accompanying water, maintains hydration and provides a substrate to spare body protein and reduce ketosis during periods of inadequate intake.

absolute: Hereditary fructose intolerance (risk of severe hypoglycemia and acute liver failure)
States of fluid overload (e.g., uncompensated heart failure, pulmonary edema) where additional fluid is hazardous
relative: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus or marked hyperglycemia
Risk of fructose accumulation (severe hepatic dysfunction)
monitor: Fluid balance and signs of overload
Infusion site and lactate/acid-base status with large loads

preg: Invert sugar solution may be used during pregnancy when fluid and caloric support is clinically indicated; monitor maternal glucose. It is not known to cause fetal harm when used appropriately, but as with any parenteral therapy, use only when clearly needed.
lact: Invert sugar infusion provides hydration and calories and is considered compatible with breastfeeding. It has no specific adverse effect on the breastfed infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment, particularly with oliguria or anuria, because of the risk of fluid overload and electrolyte disturbance. Monitor fluid balance and electrolytes and adjust the infusion rate accordingly.
hepatic: Fructose is metabolized mainly by the liver. In severe hepatic dysfunction or fructose-handling disorders, fructose can accumulate. Invert sugar is contraindicated in hereditary fructose intolerance and should be used cautiously in severe liver disease.

major: Drugs requiring fluid restriction or causing fluid retention - additive risk of overload
moderate: Insulin and oral hypoglycemics - carbohydrate load affects glucose control and dosing
Corticosteroids/diuretics - may alter glucose and electrolyte balance
minor: Medications added to the infusion - verify compatibility before mixing
interactions.food: Provides parenteral carbohydrate; coordinate with overall nutritional intake.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; chronic alcohol use may affect carbohydrate metabolism.
interactions.diagnostics: Can raise blood glucose and affect electrolyte/fluid status, relevant to laboratory monitoring during infusion.

common: Hyperglycemia and glycosuria with rapid or excessive infusion
serious: Severe hypoglycemia and acute hepatic failure in hereditary fructose intolerance
Fluid overload, pulmonary edema, and electrolyte disturbances
Hyperosmolar state and osmotic diuresis with excessive glucose load
Lactic acidosis with very large fructose loads
emergency: Acute hepatic failure/hypoglycemia in fructose intolerance
Acute pulmonary edema from fluid overload

monitoring: Fluid balance (intake/output, weight, signs of overload)
Infusion site for infiltration or phlebitis
Liver function and lactate if large carbohydrate loads are given
counsel: This is a sugar solution given through a vein to provide fluids and calories when you cannot eat or drink enough
Tell your healthcare team if you have a fructose intolerance, diabetes, kidney, or heart problems
Report any swelling, shortness of breath, or pain/redness at the drip site
Your blood sugar and fluid balance will be checked during the infusion
The rate will be controlled by your team to keep your blood sugar and fluids safe
pk: Immediate availability of glucose/fructose on intravenous infusion
Plasma glucose rises during infusion proportional to rate
Rapid metabolism/utilization of glucose and fructose
Effect limited to the infusion period and immediate metabolism
Store at room temperature; protect from freezing; do not use if cloudy or if the container is damaged
pearls: NOT a distinct branded FDA-approved drug - invert sugar is a compendial (USP-type) parenteral carbohydrate solution; this record is based on pharmacopeial/parenteral-nutrition references, and clinical use today is uncommon
Equimolar glucose + fructose (from hydrolyzed sucrose); supplies ~4 kcal/g plus water for hydration
ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in hereditary fructose intolerance - fructose causes severe hypoglycemia and acute liver failure
Control the infusion rate to avoid hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis, fluid overload, and (with large fructose loads) lactic acidosis/hyperuricemia
Monitor blood glucose, fluid balance, and electrolytes throughout the infusion
missed: Invert sugar is administered as a controlled intravenous infusion in a clinical setting; there is no patient-administered missed dose. If an infusion is interrupted, the clinical team resumes or adjusts it based on the patient's fluid, glucose, and caloric status.
overdose: Excessive infusion can cause hyperglycemia, glycosuria, osmotic diuresis with dehydration or hyperosmolar state, fluid overload, and electrolyte disturbances; large fructose loads may cause lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia. In hereditary fructose intolerance, even modest amounts can cause life-threatening hypoglycemia and hepatic failure. Management is to stop the infusion and provide supportive care, correcting glucose, fluids, and electrolytes.
